propositions.statement: Every job admitted to Orion is executed by a worker.
An execution attempt is one delivery of the job to a worker that either succeeds, fails, or times out.
A job must be executed at most three times in total.
The first execution counts as one of the three permitted executions.
When the third execution has ended without success, no further execution of that job may be started.
After an execution attempt fails, the worker must wait exactly five seconds from the end of the failed attempt before every retry.
The retry wait must not be shortened or lengthened based on the attempt number.
Each execution attempt is bounded by a timeout and must time out after thirty seconds of execution.
An attempt that reaches the timeout must be treated and recorded as a failed attempt, after which the retry policy applies.
While a job with a given job id is active, any further delivery carrying the same job id must be ignored so the job is not executed twice because of redelivery.
Ignoring a duplicate delivery must not change the state of the active job.
Each delivery may carry an idempotency key chosen by the producer.
Orion must retain each idempotency key for twenty-four hours after it is first seen so repeated deliveries with the same key can be recognised.
After the retention period the key may be forgotten and a later delivery with the same key is treated as new.
A worker that receives a job holds a lease on it, which marks the job as being worked on and prevents a second worker from taking it.
A worker lease must last sixty seconds from the moment the job is delivered to the worker.
When the lease expires without renewal or release, the job must become available to other workers.
A worker may renew its lease every thirty seconds while work on the job is progressing.
A renewal must extend the lease by the full lease duration from the moment of renewal.
A producer or operator may cancel a job.
After a job is cancelled, no future execution attempt of that job may be started.
Cancellation must not interrupt an already running execution attempt; that attempt runs to its own completion, failure, or timeout.
After the final unsuccessful execution attempt, Orion must automatically move the job to the dead-letter queue, where it can be inspected without blocking the queue.
A job in the dead-letter queue must not be executed again unless explicitly resubmitted.
When three dead-letter events occur for the same tenant within one hour, Orion must raise an operator escalation.
The one-hour escalation window must be measured from the first of the three events.
Orion guarantees ordering only where it can do so without serialising the whole service.
First-in-first-out execution order must be guaranteed only among jobs in the same queue partition.
No ordering guarantee is made between jobs in different partitions.
Every state transition of a job is recorded as an audit event.
Audit events must be retained for thirty days after they are recorded.
After thirty days an audit event may be deleted.

sentences_to_account.text: Every job admitted to Orion is executed by a worker.
An execution attempt is one delivery of the job to a worker that either succeeds, fails, or times out.
Orion bounds the number of attempts so that a job that cannot succeed does not consume worker capacity forever.
A job must be executed at most three times in total.
The first execution counts as one of the three.
When the third execution has ended without success, no further execution of that job may be started.
A job whose first two executions fail is executed a third time.
If that execution also fails, the job has exhausted its attempts.
After an execution attempt fails, Orion waits before delivering the job again.
The wait gives transient downstream faults time to clear without hammering the dependency that just failed.
Before every retry attempt the worker must wait exactly five seconds, measured from the end of the failed attempt.
The wait must not be shortened or lengthened based on the attempt number.
An attempt fails at 10:00:00.
The next attempt may start no earlier than 10:00:05.
If that attempt also fails at 10:00:20, the following attempt may start no earlier than 10:00:25.
A worker that hangs must not hold a job indefinitely.
Each attempt is bounded by a timeout after which the attempt is treated as failed and the retry policy applies.
Each execution attempt must time out after thirty seconds of execution.
An attempt that reaches the timeout must be recorded as a failed attempt.
An attempt starts at 12:00:00 and has not completed by 12:00:30.
Orion records the attempt as failed at 12:00:30.
Producers may deliver the same job more than once, for example after a network timeout on the producer side.
Orion must not execute a job twice because of such redelivery.
While a job with a given job id is active, any further delivery carrying the same job id must be ignored.
Ignoring a duplicate delivery must not change the state of the active job.
Job J-17 is delivered at 09:00 and is executing.
A second delivery of J-17 arrives at 09:01 and is ignored; J-17 continues unaffected.
Each delivery may carry an idempotency key chosen by the producer.
Orion remembers keys for a bounded period so that repeated deliveries with the same key can be recognised.
Orion must retain each idempotency key for twenty-four hours after it is first seen.
After the retention period the key may be forgotten and a later delivery with the same key is treated as new.
Key K-9 is first seen on Monday at 08:00.
A delivery with K-9 on Monday at 20:00 is recognised as a repeat.
A delivery with K-9 on Tuesday at 09:00 is treated as new.
A worker that receives a job holds a lease on it.
The lease is how Orion knows that the job is being worked on and prevents a second worker from taking it.
A worker lease must last sixty seconds from the moment the job is delivered to the worker.
When the lease expires without renewal or release, the job must become available to other workers.
A worker receives job J-4 at 14:00:00 and neither renews nor releases it.
At 14:01:00 the lease expires and J-4 may be delivered to another worker.
Long-running work must be able to keep its lease.
A worker renews the lease to signal that it is still progressing.
A worker may renew its lease every thirty seconds while work on the job is progressing.
A renewal must extend the lease by the full lease duration from the moment of renewal.
A worker holding a sixty-second lease that started at 14:00:00 renews at 14:00:30; the lease now runs until 14:01:30.
A producer or operator may cancel a job.
Cancellation stops Orion from investing further effort in the job, but Orion does not forcibly abort work that a worker is already performing.
After a job is cancelled, no future execution attempt of that job may be started.
Cancellation must not interrupt an execution attempt that is already running; that attempt runs to its own completion, failure or timeout.
Job J-8 is cancelled while its second attempt is running.
The second attempt continues; when it ends, no third attempt is started.
When a job has used all of its attempts without success, Orion must decide what happens to it.
Orion parks such jobs where they can be inspected without blocking the queue.
After the final unsuccessful execution attempt, Orion must automatically move the job to the dead-letter queue.
A job in the dead-letter queue must not be executed again unless explicitly resubmitted.
Job J-2 fails its last permitted attempt at 16:05.
Orion moves J-2 to the dead-letter queue at 16:05 without operator involvement.
Repeated dead-letter events for one tenant usually indicate a systemic fault rather than isolated bad jobs.
Orion escalates to an operator when the rate of such events crosses a threshold.
When three dead-letter events occur for the same tenant within one hour, Orion must raise an operator escalation.
The one-hour window must be measured from the first of the three events.
Tenant T-1 accumulates dead-letter events at 10:05, 10:40 and 10:55.
The third event is within one hour of the first, so an escalation is raised.
Producers sometimes depend on jobs being executed in the order they were enqueued.
Orion guarantees ordering only where it can do so without serialising the whole service.
First-in-first-out execution order must be guaranteed only among jobs in the same queue partition.
No ordering guarantee is made between jobs in different partitions.
Jobs J-10 and J-11 are enqueued in that order into partition P-3; J-10 begins execution before J-11.
Job J-12 in partition P-4 may begin before or after either.
Every state transition of a job is recorded as an audit event.
Audit events support incident investigation and tenant reporting, and are retained for a bounded period.
Audit events must be retained for thirty days after they are recorded.
After thirty days an audit event may be deleted.
An audit event recorded on 1 March may be deleted on or after 31 March.
